title: Media stocks: how to analyze media and streaming companies
description: Media stocks: the content cost is the raw material, subscribers the engine and write-downs the trap — how to analyze media companies with worked examples.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Media stocks are shares in companies that create and sell content — films, series, music and sport — not the companies owning the networks that carry it — that is telecom, a different business with its own rules ([the telecom sector](/kurser/km-046-telekomsektorn)). What separates the media company from other sectors is the raw material: a steel mill buys ore, but a media company manufactures its own raw material — and the same series can pay for itself for ten years, be written down to zero, or become a catalogue asset driving the subscriber flow. Media stock analysis therefore begins where other sector guides end: in the content cost.

AK1A's hundred-company universe carries six of them, spanning the field's range: Disney, Netflix, Spotify, Viaplay, Warner Bros. Discovery and Modern Times Group. This guide walks the three revenue engines, the content accounting, the winner and loser profiles — and the multiple chaos when earnings fail. As always here: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## Three revenue engines — the mixed economy of media stocks

Most media companies mix three revenue sources: subscriptions, advertising and tickets. Netflix and Viaplay sell subscriptions; Spotify blends paying subscribers with an ad-funded free tier; Disney carries streaming, cinema, merchandise and parks in one corporation; Warner Bros. Discovery keeps one foot in linear television, whose shrinking advertising and distribution revenue still finances part of the streaming push.

The mixed economy is an analytical key, not a detail. Three engines reacting differently to the cycle and technology shifts bring stability — but must be read segment by segment, because a growing engine can mask a shrinking one. Sports rights are a fourth gear: they lock subscribers hard, but the cost is renegotiated contract by contract — a different cost curve from own production. One-sided revenue streams are covered in [revenue diversification](/blogg/intaktsdiversifiering-risken-som-inte-syns-i-pe), subscription revenue quality — recurring and predictable — in [what recurring revenue says](/blogg/arr-tillvaxt-vad-atkommande-intakter-sager); course depth in [ARR growth](/kurser/v02-arr-tillvaxt).

## The content cost — a raw material booked as an asset

Content is produced capital-intensively and booked as an asset amortized over time — in practice an inventory refined rather than sold. Two consequences follow.

The first is scale. Netflix turned over 45.2 billion dollars in 2025 at a gross margin of 49.1 percent; Viaplay reached its peak revenue in 2023 at 18.6 billion kronor with 15.0 percent gross. The difference is the library's economics: the same catalogue serving hundreds of millions of subscribers spreads the content cost over more paying customers. Netflix's 2025 gross profit was around 22 billion dollars; Viaplay's peak-year figure just under 2.8 billion kronor. [The gross margin](/kurser/v07-bruttomarginal) is the media company's first measure.

The second is the write-downs. When content is judged not to pay for itself, the asset is written down — and the item can be enormous. Viaplay reported a 2023 loss of 9.7 billion kronor where write-downs of content and goodwill dominated; Warner Bros. Discovery went to minus 11.3 billion dollars in 2024 for the same reason and turned to plus 0.7 billion in 2025. A write-down is not a cash flow item — but it is real economics: capital laid out that never returns. The accounting is covered in [goodwill and intangible assets](/kurser/km-022-goodwill-och-immateriella-tillgangar).

## The subscriber economy — two dials and a leverage

The subscription business has two dials: subscriber count and price per subscriber. A worked example: ten million subscribers at 120 kronor monthly give 14.4 billion kronor a year. If content and technology together cost a fixed twelve billion, 2.4 billion remains in contribution. Add one million subscribers — ten percent more — and revenue grows by 1.44 billion while the fixed cost stands still: contribution rises to 3.84 billion, a full 60 percent more. That is the subscription model's operating leverage — profit moves faster than revenue. The mechanics are symmetric: when subscribers leave, the leverage turns downward the same way — which is why churn, the departure rate, is the most watched figure in streaming reports.

The real-world mechanics: Netflix's revenue climbed 2022–2025 from 31.6 to 45.2 billion dollars — 12.6 percent per year — while profit went from 4.5 to 11.0 billion. Spotify completed the whole change of sign: minus 532 million euro in 2023 to plus 2,212 million in 2025. Disney, with parks and cinema beside streaming, went from 2.4 billion dollars profit in 2023 to 12.4 billion in 2025.

A fourth variant is pure one-off pedagogy: MTG's 2022 profit of 6.5 billion kronor came not from operations but from divesting the entertainment business; the year after, profit fell to 0.2 billion, then to losses. Organic versus acquired development is mandatory reading — [organic versus acquired growth](/kurser/tx-01-organisk-mot-forvarvad-tillvaxt) — and the items live in [the notes](/kurser/km-004-noter).

## Winners and losers — the balance sheet decides

The media sector showed both extremes within one industry in 2022–2025. Netflix and Spotify carry debt-to-equity of 0.55 and 0.06 respectively, Disney 0.39 — financed expansions that have matured. Viaplay's debt-to-equity landed at 3.30 after the loss years, and the way out was new share issues: existing owners subscribed or were diluted — the mechanics in [the emission risk](/kurser/rk-02-emissionrisk), the capital consumption in [capital burn](/kurser/v19-kapitalforbranning). Return on equity spans from Netflix's 49.5 and Spotify's 44.5 percent to Viaplay's minus 52.9 — mirror images of one business model at different library scale. Debt-to-equity levels are walked through in [which level is dangerous](/blogg/skuldsattningsgrad-vilken-niva-ar-farlig), solidity measures in [solidity and interest coverage](/kurser/st-01-soliditet-och-rantetackning).

## The multiple chaos — when P/E fails

When profit is negative or zero, the P/E ratio lacks its denominator: Warner Bros. Discovery and Viaplay lack P/E in the universe's data though both are alive. The comparison moves to book value and revenue — the ranges are enormous: Netflix trades at 11.4 times book value, Warner Bros. Discovery at 2.2 and MTG at 1.4. The difference is the return on capital: a high P/B is justified only by high, sustainable return on equity — the relationship in [how do you calculate ROE](/blogg/hur-raknar-man-roe) and [the P/B ratio](/kurser/v05-pb).

The most misleading figure is cash flow: Warner Bros. Discovery reported a free cash flow margin of 44.8 percent in the same year as its 2024 loss. Write-downs are not cash flow, so the company generates cash while the income statement is red — but living cash does not mean the capital is being repaid. Multiple choice in missing-profit situations: [EV/Sales](/kurser/vm-08-evsales), [multiple choice](/kurser/vm-03-multipelval) and [when P/S is useful](/blogg/ps-tal-nar-ar-det-anvandbart). PEG, setting the multiple against growth, has its own pitfalls — MTG's combination of P/E 93.6 and PEG 0.52 explains why in [the weaknesses of the PEG multiple](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026).

## How to read the media company's report — five points

- **Subscribers and ARPU.** Count, price per subscriber and churn per service — decides whether the engine is volume or price.
- **The content cost.** Production, amortization and write-downs; the gross margin is always counted first.
- **The segments one by one.** Streaming, linear television, cinema and parks — a growing engine can mask a shrinking one.
- **Cash flow against profit.** Cash can live while profit is dictated by write-downs — read both, with [EV/EBITDA](/blogg/vad-ar-ev-ebitda) as the bridge.
- **One-offs.** Divestments and restructurings — the MTG case: a record profit carried by a sale that never returns.

The full reading order: [the quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten).

## The summary

- The media company manufactures its own raw material: the content cost is booked as an asset, amortized — and written down by the billion when needed (Viaplay −9.7 billion kronor 2023, Warner Bros. Discovery −11.3 billion dollars 2024).
- Three revenue engines — subscriptions, advertising, tickets — should be read segment by segment.
- The subscription leverage: in the worked example, ten percent more subscribers gave 60 percent higher contribution.
- P/E fails at negative profit — the multiple chaos is resolved with P/B against return and EV/Sales, with cash flow as the reality check.
- The balance sheet separates winners from losers: debt-to-equity 0.06–0.55 against 3.30, return on equity +49.5 against −52.9 percent.
